title: Skin layers, glands and functions
blurb: Order the epidermal layers, tell the dermis from the hypodermis, match each gland to its secretion and explain what skin does.
question: On a hot run, Sofia's skin turns flushed and damp. Which glands are producing the sweat, where do they open, and what are her dermal blood vessels doing?

teach.body: Formally, the integumentary system is the skin (epidermis and dermis) together with hair, nails, glands and sensory receptors; the hypodermis beneath it is technically not skin. In plain English: skin is a living, layered wrapping, and by both area and weight it is the largest organ. The outer epidermis is a tough, waterproof sheet of cells; the dermis underneath supplies strength, blood, nerves and glands.

children.label: Dermis
children.sub: connective tissue; vessels, nerves, follicles, glands

teach.caption: The epidermis has no blood vessels: it is fed by diffusion from the dermis below.

steps.label: Stratum basale
steps.sub: Deepest: dividing stem cells, melanocytes, Merkel cells

steps.label: Stratum granulosum
steps.sub: Keratinization begins; cells start to die

steps.label: Stratum lucidum
steps.sub: Clear layer: thick skin of palms and soles only

steps.label: Stratum corneum
steps.sub: Many layers of dead, flat, keratin-filled cells; shed

teach.caption: New cells take about 4 weeks to move from the basale to the surface.

Makes or does
Layer
teach.caption: Skin color comes from melanin, carotene (yellow-orange) and hemoglobin (pink). People differ in how much melanin they make, not in melanocyte numbers.
Collagen gives strength; elastin gives stretch and recoil. Subcutaneous injections go into the hypodermis.
Apocrine odor comes from bacteria breaking down the sweat. Earwax (ceruminous) and mammary glands are modified sweat glands.

head: Function
How
rows: Barrier, keratin, acid mantle, melanin vs UV, immune cells
Sweat; dermal vessels dilate to lose heat, constrict to keep it
UVB makes a precursor; liver and kidneys activate it
Salts and urea in sweat; lipid-soluble drugs, patches

teach.body: Sofia jogs on a hot afternoon. Her eccrine glands pour watery sweat through pores onto the skin surface, and evaporation cools her. Her dermal blood vessels dilate, bringing warm blood close to the surface to release heat, which is why she looks flushed. Meanwhile the UVB in sunlight converts a cholesterol derivative in her skin to vitamin D3, which her liver and kidneys later convert to active calcitriol.

teach.text: The epidermis is AVASCULAR. Stratum basale is deepest and corneum is outermost; the lucidum is in THICK skin only. ECCRINE glands cool the body and open onto the surface; APOCRINE glands open into hair follicles. Keratin waterproofs; melanin is the pigment. Skin makes only a vitamin D PRECURSOR.

items: Epidermis (avascular epithelium), dermis (vascular connective tissue), hypodermis (fat; not true skin).
Deep to superficial: basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin), corneum.
Keratinocytes make keratin; melanocytes in the basale make melanin.
Eccrine: watery sweat, surface pores, cooling. Apocrine: follicles, armpits, puberty. Sebaceous: sebum.
Functions: protection, thermoregulation, sensation, vitamin D precursor, minor excretion and absorption.

summary: You can now order the epidermal layers, place each cell type and receptor, and distinguish the papillary dermis, reticular dermis and hypodermis. You can also match eccrine, apocrine and sebaceous glands to their secretions and explain how skin protects, regulates temperature and starts vitamin D production.

A.q: Which epidermal layer is deepest and contains the dividing stem cells?
A.why: The stratum basale (germinativum) is a single row of dividing stem cells at the base of the epidermis.

whyNot.0: The stratum corneum is the outermost layer of dead, keratin-filled cells.
whyNot.1: The stratum spinosum lies just above the basale and holds Langerhans cells.
whyNot.3: The stratum granulosum is where keratinization begins and cells start to die.

A.q: Which cells produce the pigment that absorbs ultraviolet light and protects DNA?
A.why: Melanocytes in the stratum basale make melanin, which absorbs UV radiation.

whyNot.0: Keratinocytes make keratin, a waterproofing protein, not the UV pigment.
whyNot.2: Langerhans (dendritic) cells play an immune role.

A.q: Which statement about the epidermis is correct?
options: It has no blood vessels of its own
It is made of dense connective tissue
It holds the hair follicles and sweat glands
Its deepest layer is the stratum corneum
A.why: The epidermis is avascular; its cells are nourished by diffusion from the dermis.

whyNot.1: The epidermis is stratified squamous epithelium; the dermis is connective tissue.
whyNot.2: Hair follicles and glands sit in the dermis.
whyNot.3: The stratum corneum is the outermost layer; the basale is deepest.

B.q: Which gland type is most numerous, releases watery sweat through pores and is the main cooler of the body?
B.why: Eccrine (merocrine) glands are found all over the body and secrete watery sweat onto the surface for thermoregulation.

whyNot.0: Apocrine glands open into hair follicles in the armpits and anogenital area and are not the main coolers.
whyNot.2: Sebaceous glands secrete oily sebum, not sweat.
whyNot.3: Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands that make earwax.

B.q: Where is the stratum lucidum found?
options: Thin skin over most of the body
All skin, just beneath the corneum
Skin of the scalp and face
Thick skin of palms and soles
B.why: The clear stratum lucidum is present in the thick skin of the palms and soles.

whyNot.0: Thin skin, which covers most of the body, has no stratum lucidum.
whyNot.1: It does sit just beneath the corneum, but in thick skin, not in all skin.
whyNot.2: The scalp and face are covered by thin skin, which lacks this layer.

B.q: Which statement best describes the skin's role in vitamin D production?
options: It makes active calcitriol without help from other organs
It absorbs ready-made vitamin D from sunlight
It stores vitamin D made by the liver in its fat
It makes a precursor that the liver and kidneys activate
B.why: UVB converts a cholesterol derivative in the skin to vitamin D3; the liver and kidneys convert it to active calcitriol.

whyNot.0: Skin makes the precursor; activation to calcitriol requires the liver and kidneys.
whyNot.1: Sunlight supplies UVB energy, not vitamin D itself; the skin makes the precursor.
whyNot.2: The liver does not make vitamin D for the skin to store; the skin starts the process.

C.q: Sofia jogs on a hot afternoon. Which pair of skin responses helps her lose heat?
options: Apocrine sweating and constriction of dermal vessels
Sebum secretion and dilation of dermal vessels
Eccrine sweating and dilation of dermal vessels
Eccrine sweating and constriction of dermal vessels
C.why: Eccrine sweat cools by evaporation, and dilated dermal vessels bring warm blood to the surface to release heat.

whyNot.0: Apocrine glands are not the thermoregulators, and constricted vessels conserve heat.
whyNot.1: Sebum lubricates skin and hair; it does not cool the body.
whyNot.3: Constricting dermal vessels conserves heat, the opposite of what Sofia needs.

C.q: Which layers are damaged in a second-degree (partial-thickness) burn?
options: Epidermis and all of the dermis
Epidermis and part of the dermis
C.why: A second-degree burn involves the epidermis and part of the dermis, which is why it blisters.

whyNot.0: Damage confined to the epidermis is a first-degree (superficial) burn.
whyNot.1: Damage through the whole dermis is a third-degree (full-thickness) burn.
whyNot.2: Damage extending through the dermis and below is full thickness, not partial.

C.q: Which statement explains why people with darker skin have darker pigmentation?
options: They have many more melanocytes per area
Their stratum corneum holds more hemoglobin
C.why: Melanocyte numbers are similar between people; darker skin reflects more melanin production.

whyNot.1: People have similar numbers of melanocytes; the amount of melanin made differs.
whyNot.2: Carotene adds a yellow-orange tint but is not the main source of skin darkness.
whyNot.3: Hemoglobin is in dermal blood, adding pink tones; the dead corneum holds no blood.

reteach.title: A wall that builds itself from the bottom up
reteach.question: Imagine a wall where new bricks are made only at the bottom row and slowly pushed up until the top ones crumble off. How does that match the epidermis?

blocks.body: The stratum basale is the brick factory at the bottom. New cells are pushed upward over about 4 weeks, filling with keratin and dying as they rise, until they become the flat, dead roof tiles of the stratum corneum that flake off. The wall has no pipes of its own: plumbing (blood vessels), wiring (nerves), sprinklers (sweat glands) and oilers (sebaceous glands) all live in the dermis foundation beneath.

blocks.text: The roof is dead and the factory is at the bottom: basale deepest, corneum outermost.

explain.body: Stratified squamous keratinized epithelium with no blood vessels. Deep to superficial: basale (stem cells, melanocytes, Merkel cells), spinosum (Langerhans cells), granulosum (keratinization begins), lucidum (thick skin only), corneum (dead keratinized cells).

test.q: Langerhans (dendritic) cells, which serve an immune role, are found mainly in which layer?
test.why: Langerhans cells sit in the stratum spinosum, where they act as immune sentinels.

whyNot.0: The stratum basale holds stem cells, melanocytes and Merkel cells.
whyNot.2: The stratum granulosum is where keratinization begins and cells start to die.
whyNot.3: The stratum corneum consists of dead keratinized cells.

explain.body: The papillary dermis (areolar tissue) has dermal papillae that form fingerprints, capillary loops and Meissner corpuscles. The reticular dermis (dense irregular tissue) holds collagen and elastin. The hypodermis is fat and areolar tissue for insulation, energy storage and cushioning.

test.q: Which layer forms the ridges that create fingerprints?
test.why: Dermal papillae of the papillary layer push up the epidermis into friction ridges, the fingerprints.

whyNot.1: The reticular layer is the deeper, collagen-rich part of the dermis.
whyNot.2: The hypodermis is a fatty layer beneath the skin.
whyNot.3: The stratum basale follows the ridges but does not create them; the dermal papillae do.

explain.body: Eccrine glands release watery sweat onto the surface for cooling. Apocrine glands in the armpits and anogenital area open into hair follicles and become active at puberty. Sebaceous glands secrete sebum, usually into hair follicles, and are absent from palms and soles.

test.q: Which glands secrete sebum, usually into hair follicles?
test.why: Sebaceous (oil) glands secrete sebum, which lubricates skin and hair and slows water loss.

whyNot.0: Eccrine glands secrete watery sweat onto the skin surface.
whyNot.1: Apocrine glands open into hair follicles but secrete a thicker sweat, not sebum.

explain.body: Skin protects (barrier, keratin, acid mantle, melanin, immune cells), regulates temperature (sweat and dermal blood flow), senses, makes a vitamin D precursor, excretes small amounts of salts and urea, and absorbs some lipid-soluble substances.

test.q: Which is NOT a function of the skin?
test.why: Red blood cells are produced in red bone marrow, not in the skin.

whyNot.0: UVB converts a cholesterol derivative in skin into the vitamin D precursor.
whyNot.1: Sweating and changes in dermal blood flow regulate temperature.
whyNot.2: Sweat carries small amounts of salts and urea out of the body.
